newsitem.title: USA: US lawmaker says Huang breached national security.
newsitem.headline: US lawmaker says Huang breached national security.

text.p: A Republican congressman alleged on Thursday that John Huang, a central figure in the Democratic fund-raising controversy, passed classified information to the Asian corporation where he used to work.
Rep. Gerald Solomon of New York, who chairs the House of Representatives Rules Committee, said he had received reports from "government sources" whom he declined to identify.

According to a statement released by Solomon, the sources said "electronic intercepts" existed which provided evidence that Huang, a former Commerce Department official, breached national security by passing information to his former employer, the Indonesian-based Lippo Group.
Solomon also wrote to FBI Director Louis Freeh asking if damage assessment procedures were under way to determine how seriously U.S. security was compromised.
Solomon alleged Huang had access to classified White House information as well as State Department message traffic through his government computer.

Huang left the Commerce Department in 1995 to become a Democratic Party fund-raiser. His fund raising and connections to Asian business have been a major part of the political scandal that has forced Democrats to return more than $1 million in possibly illegal contributions.

Democratic sources said they were unimpressed by Solomon's claim. "This is a potentially explosive development but who are these sources? We are certainly not privy to any such information. If he has the goods, let's see them," said one.

In a separate development, Republicans and Democrats on a Senate committee conducting its own investigation into fund-raising scandals prepared for a confrontation later on Thursday over Republican demands that 19 witnesses be offered immunity from prosecution in exchange for their testimony.

Democrats on the Governmental Affairs Committee said they would block the immunity offers because Republicans were treating the investigation as a witch hunt of Democrats. Republicans need the votes of at least two of the seven Democrats on the committee to proceed.

Huang has emerged as a central figure in the scandal in which Asian business interests and the government of China are suspected of attempting to gain influence by funneling illegal funds to President Bill Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign and the Democratic National Committee.
He has refused to cooperate with the various investigations under way by invoking his right under the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution not to incriminate himself.

Huang was the top U.S. representative of the Lippo Group, a vast financial conglomerate with close ties to China. He was appointed a deputy assistant secretary at Commerce in the Clinton administration in late 1993 and given a top-secret security clearance.
In that capacity, he attended numerous classified briefings at which U.S. trade strategy and policies were discussed. Meanwhile, he stayed in close touch with Lippo.
In December 1995, Huang moved to the Democratic Party where he began organizing a fund-raising drive to bring in millions of dollars from Asian Americans.
The DNC subsequently had to return $1.5 million raised by Huang because of suspicions that it came from foreign sources, which is illegal under U.S. law.
